quoted.text:
This is the new Tesla Roadster's fan and suction system, which the company filed a patent for in April 2025.

Sides skirts and front and rear skirts deploy under the battery pack, sucking the car down at ~2G. Because the skirts can move, they have some compliance, so they can deal with road bumps, road debris, etc. As the speed of the Roadster increases, the front and rear skirts retract to allow for air-flow (venturi effect) under the vehicle.

Tesla: "Our multi-mode fan and ground sealing system acts as a downforce generator, pulling air out from beneath the vehicle. This provides enough suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary. Powered fans and active wings maximize traction and cornering speeds in all conditions, achieving massive downforce at zero speed."

In their patent, Tesla said: "In the first mode, a complete set of skirts creates a fully sealed bounded region under the vehicle with central fans generating maximum downforce at low speeds on smooth surfaces. In the second mode, a subset of skirts (primarily side skirts) modifies the bounded region while all fans operate to provide downforce in dynamic driving conditions with uneven surfaces. The system includes a control mechanism to selectively deploy skirts and operate fans based on driving conditions, optimizing between maximum downforce at low speeds and improved performance over varying terrain at higher speeds."

posts.name: Kris Sidial🇺🇸
posts.text:
Very often, I’ll speak to allocators who have target return objectives for their investments. I usually express that I’m not a fan of this approach, particularly when it comes to long volatility strategies.

Let me explain why.

Imagine you have a friend who tells you, “Hey, I’m a good poker player. I’m going to play at this casino tonight, and I’m not leaving until I make $500K.”

He starts with a bankroll of $50K. He’s a skilled player, and fortunately, he’s seated at a table with players who are considerably worse than him.

Nine hours go by, and he’s now up $450K. However, the table dynamics change. A few players rotate out, and two players he recognizes from other circuits sit down. He knows both are significantly better than him.

To me, a good poker player would recognize that the opportunity set has deteriorated. He might play a few more hands with a strict floor in mind, but if that floor is breached, he picks up his chips and calls it a night.

Unfortunately, our friend has committed himself to his original rule: He cannot leave until he makes $500K.

So he continues playing. Nine hours later, he has lost everything.

Now, let’s change the scenario.

Instead of two superior players joining the table, imagine two more fish sit down. Our friend plays another hour, makes the additional $50K, reaches his $500K target, and walks away.

Unfortunately, those two fish each have an additional $2M bankroll and are willing to keep playing all night.

In the first scenario, had he recognized the deterioration in the opportunity set, he could have walked away with $450K instead of nothing.

In the second scenario, had he recognized the improvement in the opportunity set, he might have walked away with $2M instead of $500K.

So what went wrong in both scenarios?

He allowed an arbitrary return target to dictate his decisions rather than the underlying conditions that actually determined his expected profitability.

This is the fundamental problem I have with target-based investment frameworks.

When you establish external parameters that have no meaningful relationship to the underlying distribution of outcomes, you risk systematically making the wrong decisions. You end up taking too much risk when the opportunity set deteriorates and taking too little when it improves.

Now, bring this back to volatility investing.

I often speak with allocators who say things like, “We want our hedging program to generate a 40% return if the market declines 20%, and we want to monetize when that happens.”

I try my best to explain that the parameters you establish for your hedging program have absolutely no influence on the path the market takes or the opportunity set that develops along the way.

A 20% market decline tells you very little, in isolation, about whether the remaining convexity is attractively priced, whether volatility is likely to continue expanding, or whether the positioning dynamics that created the opportunity have been exhausted.

This is precisely why so many hedging programs struggle with monetization. They either monetize too early, leaving substantial profits on the table, or monetize too late, allowing significant gains to evaporate.

The problem isn’t necessarily the hedge itself. It’s that the decision to monetize is being driven by an arbitrary objective rather than the variables that actually determine the expected value of continuing to hold the position.

The objective should never be to maximize returns relative to an arbitrary target. It should be to maximize the value extracted from the opportunity set as it evolves.

Really enjoyed You Can See Everything. Might be most meta documentary ever.  

No spoilers but will say this interview Christopher Nolan did with Nathan Fielder about his show “The Curse” — explaining his creative process — really comes through in Holmes film:

▫️setting the tone is his top priority, even moreso than narrative (“when you have the tone right, everything falls into place”) 

▫️Fielder says he “stumbles into ideas he gets excited about” without a master plan and “just piles things on and it grows” (for the Holmes doc, he had an agreement with A24 to scrap the project even after years of shooting if he didn’t think there was a film)

▫️the musical score is crucial in setting the tone (the sound doesn’t even have to match action on the scene, it can float above just setting mood)

▫️he doesn’t want to rush scenes; let them develop to the point where audience is expecting any action to be consequential and it builds the tension (inspired by old detective TV show Columbo)

***

Full interview here (Nolan really is a Fielder Stan): https://youtu.be/etoG2I6gaHE?si=SPNzDV9H5O5NG90S

Non-asset owners are seeing a large drop in US consumer sentiment.

Since January 2026, consumer sentiment is down -27% among the bottom 33% of stockholders, the largest decline among the stock-wealth groups surveyed.

This is followed by those who do not own stocks, whose sentiment is down -25% over the same period.

By comparison, sentiment is down just -9% among the middle 33% and -7% among the top 33% of stockholders.

Asset ownership has helped offset the impact of higher living costs, leaving consumers with fewer or no stocks more exposed to the recent acceleration in inflation.

Meanwhile, 1-year consumer inflation expectations rose +0.1 percentage point this month, to 4.7%, its 2nd-highest reading since August 2025.

Own assets or be left behind.

"Gold is one of those things that even though it's the same asset, it's not treated the same based on where it is."

"If you tell somebody you have a million dollars worth of gold in a vault in Switzerland, they react very differently than you say you have a million dollars worth of gold in a vault in Venezuela or in Zimbabwe."

"How much can I borrow with my gold that's in Venezuela? The answer will be zero. Or you would have to basically find a person comfortable with lending you anything using Venezuelan gold as collateral."

"Because different countries have different property rights, different regulatory risks, different corruption regimes."

"Tokenized gold addresses this problem, which is to say, let's keep the gold in the highest quality vaults in a very high quality property rights government like the Swiss government in a Swiss vault, the highest of standards, and let's give everybody a token receipt of the gold in that vault."

posts.text:
Some impressions from the Bank-Fund meetings in Bangkok:

1. The words are all negative but the numbers are all positive. Is all about unprecedented waves of shocks and risks while the IMF upgraded the forecast to something even stronger.

2. No one cares about tariffs anymore, they expect them to continue forever and have adjusted and moved on.

3. Everyone cares a lot about high interest rates. They expect them to continue forever but they haven't moved on.

4. Oil prices fall somewhere between these two. Everyone cares some, aren't sure if they'll continue and have partially moved on.

5. Everyone is having exactly the same conversations about AI as they are having here: will the demand boost continue, is it a bubble, will it kill jobs, when will it show up in productivity. I sensed much more optimism than pessimism and finance ministers and central bankers are not particuarly interested in p(doom).

6. No one seemed to mind that Scott Bessent didn't bother to attend.

Pumpkin seed oil has the strongest data: oral trials showed ~40% hair count gains in men with AGA vs 10% placebo; topical animal and some female studies also positive, likely via 5α-reductase effects. 
Lavender oil promoted follicle growth in mice comparable to minoxidil in one study. 
Rosehip oil shifted mouse follicles to anagen phase. 
Sandalwood (esp. synthetic analogs) activates OR2AT4 receptors to prolong anagen and cut shedding in limited human data. 
Bakuchiol has early/in-vitro hints plus traditional use. 
Others mainly support scalp moisture/antioxidants. 
These are incidental; the serum is formulated and dosed for face skin, not scalp hair loss.

Now a jury has awarded David $6 million for defamation and tortious interference. The Boston Globe and The New York Times soon after reported the outcome. Science despite running countless negative articles shaming David is nowhere to be found today.

Science repeatedly portrayed David’s efforts in court as futile or unsuccessful by emphasizing selected pretrial rulings on court motions while significant claims were still awaiting trial. Those decisions did not determine the outcome of the claims the jury has now decided.

This goes beyond leaving out part of the story. Relentlessly publishing damaging allegations fuels the public shaming and online bullying of a person. That carries a responsibility to give a verdict in his favor comparable visibility—and to account for the narrative those articles helped establish.

David has lived with the consequences of this coverage for years. Science owes him a prominent account of this verdict and a serious reckoning with its own role in the spectacle.
